narrative:
Your law school application was denied because the model estimated a 60% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, that means failure was predicted to be more likely than success, so your application was treated as too risky to approve.

The prediction was driven mainly by three factors, ranked by influence. Your admission test score was the single most important factor, but it actually worked in your favor: at 40, it is above the average of 37.18 among accepted students, so it pushed the estimate toward passing. The second most important factor was your undergraduate GPA, which pushed strongly toward failure: 2.50 is well below the accepted-student average of 3.23. The third most important factor was your third-year class standing, which also pushed toward failure: your third-year decile of 3.00 is below the accepted-student average of 5.79. Together, the weaker GPA and class standing outweighed the positive signal from your admission test score, leaving the model at a 60% failure estimate.

To improve a future application, focus on building stronger evidence of academic readiness: raise your GPA through additional coursework if possible, improve your academic standing, and meet with admissions or prelaw advising to create a concrete remediation plan. Because your admission test score is already a relative strength, prioritize sustained academic performance and documented progress before reapplying.
